title: Untitled
medium: Graphite, colored pencils, and watercolor on paper
altText: A wide drawing on paper made with pencil, colored pencils and watercolor, in the quick, energetic line of Jean-Michel Basquiat. The museum's subject tags list masks and elephants; other details have not been confirmed from the record.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record and public object page: title, artist, date, medium, public-domain flag (false), empty image fields, credit line (Gift of the Estate of the artist, 1992), classification (Drawings), tags (Masks, Elephants) and dimensions (29 3/4 x 42 in.) read from the record. The page has no description of the imagery. No image linked because the work is in copyright.

context: A 1986 drawing by Jean-Michel Basquiat, an artist born in Brooklyn, New York, who first became known for street writing in the late 1970s. The Met's record lists graphite, colored pencils and watercolor on paper, and tags it with masks and elephants. The museum page offers no description of the drawing.

descriptions.k: Jean-Michel Basquiat made this drawing with pencil, colored pencils, and watercolor. The museum says it has masks and elephants in it. Can you find an elephant shape? Can you find a mask? What colors do you notice?
descriptions.g12: Jean-Michel Basquiat drew this picture on a wide piece of paper with pencil, colored pencils, and watercolor paint. The museum's tags say there are masks and elephants. His drawings often look quick and full of energy. Can you find an elephant? Can you find a mask? What do they make you feel?
descriptions.g35: Jean-Michel Basquiat grew up in Brooklyn, New York, and began as a street artist before becoming famous for paintings and drawings. This untitled drawing from 1986 uses graphite, colored pencils, and watercolor on paper about 42 inches wide. The Met tags it with masks and elephants. Search for those shapes. Why might an artist who drew quickly choose images like masks and animals?
descriptions.g68: Basquiat made this untitled drawing in 1986, using graphite, colored pencils, and watercolor on a sheet roughly 30 by 42 inches. The Met's tags list masks and elephants, but the museum offers no explanation. Basquiat's work often mixes drawn figures, symbols, and words with a rough, energetic line. What can you learn by looking for the elephants and masks, and what do you still not know without a description?
descriptions.g910: Untitled (1986) shows Basquiat working on paper with graphite, colored pencils, and watercolor, a combination that allows both rapid, scratchy line and washes of color. The Met's tags identify masks and elephants as subjects, yet give no interpretation. Basquiat's art is known for drawing together symbols, faces, and animals in a spontaneous style, and viewers debate how to read such images. Consider what the repeated motifs might suggest and which readings the evidence in the drawing can support.
descriptions.g1112: Basquiat's 1986 Untitled is a large work on paper in which line, color, and tagged imagery of masks and elephants invite interpretation. The Met supplies only basic data and subject tags, so claims about its meaning should be explicit about what is inferred. Some viewers connect his masks and animals to ideas of identity, performance, and cultural memory; others emphasize the improvisational, drawn surface. How much weight should the artist's reputation carry compared with the visible evidence of the sheet itself?

k.daily: Find an elephant shape and a mask shape. Where are they?
k.emotion: Does this drawing feel quiet or full of energy to you? What do you see that tells you?
k.observation: Which colors can you find? Point to a pencil line and a watery paint area.
k.analysis: Where do your eyes go first on this wide paper? Why do you think that is?
k.line: Are the pencil lines smooth, jumpy, or messy? Draw one in the air.
k.shape: An elephant has a big body and a long trunk. How can you find that shape here?
k.color: Which colored pencil marks stand out the most to you?
k.texture: Pencil makes scratchy lines and watercolor makes soft patches. Where can you spot each one?
k.space: Is the drawing crowded or empty? Point to a spot with lots going on.
k.light: Which parts of the drawing look lighter, and which look darker?
k.meaning: Masks hide faces. Why might an artist draw masks?
k.culture: Elephants live in places like Africa and Asia. Where have you seen elephants in pictures or stories?
k.technique: Basquiat used pencils and watercolor on the same page. What happens when you draw with both?
k.personal: If you drew an elephant and a mask, how would you make yours different?
k.critical: The museum does not say what the picture means. How can you find out more by looking?

g12.daily: Look for an elephant and a mask. What do you notice about how they are drawn?
g12.emotion: What feeling do the scribbly lines and the colors give you? Show us the part that causes it.
g12.observation: List what you see: lines, colors, shapes, and any elephant or mask you find.
g12.analysis: How does the artist fill the wide sheet of paper? Does the drawing feel crowded or open?
g12.line: Compare thin pencil lines with thick colored marks. How do they work together?
g12.shape: Basquiat's shapes can look rough and not perfect. How does that change how you see an elephant or a mask?
g12.color: Which colors are in this drawing? How do they help the shapes stand out?
g12.texture: Pencil, colored pencil, and watercolor each make a different look. Where do you see each kind?
g12.space: Basquiat drew on a wide sheet of paper. How does the shape of the paper affect the drawing?
g12.light: Where do the colors look bright and where do they look soft?
g12.meaning: The museum tags this drawing with masks and elephants. What stories do those two things make you imagine?
g12.culture: Basquiat grew up in New York City. How might the busy city have inspired his quick, energetic drawing?
g12.technique: Colored pencil and watercolor are easy to carry and use quickly. Why might Basquiat like using them?
g12.personal: If you drew a mask for yourself, what would it look like?
g12.critical: How neat does a drawing have to be to count as art? Use details from this one in your answer.

g35.daily: What parts of the drawing grab your attention first, and what choices by Basquiat cause that?
g35.emotion: How would you describe the mood of the drawing? Which lines and colors create it?
g35.observation: Take a quiet minute. Which small details did you notice late, in line, color, or shape?
g35.analysis: How does Basquiat arrange masks, animals, and marks across the wide paper?
g35.line: Basquiat is known for a quick, scratchy line. How would you describe the lines in this drawing?
g35.shape: How do the shapes of elephants and masks differ from the shapes of other marks?
g35.color: How do the colored pencils and watercolor add to the graphite lines?
g35.texture: How do graphite, colored pencils, and watercolor each leave a different mark on the paper?
g35.space: How does the artist use the whole sheet? Where does the drawing feel busy or open?
g35.light: Where do lighter watercolor areas and darker pencil marks contrast?
g35.meaning: The museum says the drawing has masks and elephants. What might each image suggest to you?
g35.culture: Basquiat began by writing on city walls before he exhibited in galleries. How might that background show in a drawing like this?
g35.technique: Why might an artist combine pencil with watercolor in one drawing?
g35.personal: What animals or masks matter to you or your family, and how might you draw them?
g35.critical: The museum gives few facts about this drawing. How can you form a careful idea about it without a description?

g68.daily: How does Basquiat's drawing style make you work to find and understand the images in it?
g68.emotion: How does the rough, fast line create a mood of urgency or play?
g68.observation: Describe how you find masks and elephants in the drawing. Which clues help most?
g68.analysis: How does the arrangement across the wide sheet guide your eyes from one image to another?
g68.line: How does Basquiat's scratchy, confident line make his figures look alive?
g68.shape: How do simplified, uneven shapes express character instead of realistic detail?
g68.color: How do colored pencils and watercolor add emphasis to the graphite drawing?
g68.texture: How does the mix of media create a surface that feels spontaneous?
g68.space: How does he use a wide, flat sheet without a realistic background?
g68.light: How do darker and lighter areas create contrast without realistic shading?
g68.meaning: Masks and elephants appear in the museum's tags. How could each be read as a symbol, and why must you be careful about that?
g68.culture: How does Basquiat's background in street art and New York culture connect to this drawing's energy?
g68.technique: What do you think are the strengths of drawing in a quick, direct way instead of planning every detail?
g68.personal: What do you draw when you want to work fast and let ideas come out?
g68.critical: How would you decide between several interpretations of a drawing when the artist gave no explanation?

g910.daily: How do the rough drawn line and the tagged motifs of masks and elephants shape your first interpretation?
g910.emotion: How does the improvisational line produce urgency or play, and how does color modify the effect?
g910.observation: Analyze the visual hierarchy: which marks, motifs, or colors lead the eye across the sheet?
g910.analysis: Analyze how Basquiat organizes figures and marks on a wide sheet without a conventional perspective.
g910.line: How does the quality of line, quick, scratchy, and direct, carry personality and energy?
g910.shape: How does the distortion or simplification of forms convey meaning beyond likeness?
g910.color: How does color overlay work with the pencil structure of the drawing?
g910.texture: In what ways do the combined media create contrasts of crispness and softness?
g910.space: How does the flat, all-over use of the page relate to Basquiat's street-art background?
g910.light: How does value contrast give the drawing structure when it lacks realistic modeling?
g910.meaning: How might masks and elephants function symbolically in Basquiat's wider work, and where does interpretation become speculative?
g910.culture: How does the drawing reflect the 1980s New York art scene and Basquiat's place within it?
g910.technique: What does the choice of works on paper reveal about immediacy and process in Basquiat's practice?
g910.personal: How does your own approach to quick, uncensored drawing compare with his?
g910.critical: How should viewers weigh biographical lore about a famous artist against what is visible in a single sheet?

g1112.daily: What argument can you make from the visible evidence of line, color, and tagged imagery about this drawing's concerns?
g1112.emotion: How does the drawing's improvisational surface complicate any attempt to assign a single emotion?
g1112.observation: Describe the sheet precisely, separating what you observe from what the museum tags tell you.
g1112.analysis: Analyze how the drawing's lack of a fixed hierarchy creates an all-over, continuous field of attention.
g1112.line: How does the line operate as both image and mark, and how does that relate to drawing as an act?
g1112.shape: How do distortion and compression of forms position the drawing within Neo-Expressionist figuration?
g1112.color: How does the interplay of colored pencil and watercolor complicate the primacy of drawn line?
g1112.texture: What does the visible layering of media suggest about process and revision?
g1112.space: How does the drawing's frontal, flat space resemble a surface to be written on, and what does that imply?
g1112.light: How is contrast, rather than modeled light, used to structure the sheet?
g1112.meaning: Evaluate readings of masks and elephants as emblems of identity, performance, or memory against a formal reading. What evidence supports each?
g1112.culture: How might the shift from street writing to museum drawing complicate the reception of Basquiat's work, and what is at stake in how institutions frame it?
g1112.technique: How does working on paper with mixed media differ in implications from large canvas painting for the artist's public image?
g1112.personal: How do your own assumptions about a celebrated artist influence what you expect to see in a drawing like this?
g1112.critical: What would be a responsible way to interpret an untitled work when the museum offers only tags and technical data?

safety.method: Title, tags (Masks, Elephants), classification (Drawings) and medium checked against the Met record; the tags list no concerning terms (no skulls, violence or nudity). The record has no description of the imagery, so student text refers only to the tagged masks and elephants. The image file itself was not visually inspected. Basquiat drawings can include text or unexpected imagery, so a person must confirm the image in the review tool before release and adjust the text to what is actually shown.

teacherNote.context: A 1986 untitled drawing by Jean-Michel Basquiat in the Met's collection, tagged with masks and elephants. The museum page gives no description, so this entry is cautious. A person must review the image before use. The work is in copyright, so no image is linked yet.
directions: Have students draw quickly for two minutes with pencil and then add a wash of watercolor, comparing it to a slow, careful drawing.
Ask students to separate what they see from what they are told by the museum tags, then list questions the tags do not answer.
Discuss why artists sometimes leave works untitled and how that changes our viewing.
